https://nineoclock.ro/russian-citizen-ar.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Romania has arrested a Russian man for spying on its military bases, thwarting an attempted sabotage plot. A Russian citizen accused of preparing acts of hybrid sabotage targeting military objectives in Romania has been placed under 30-day pre-trial arrest, following a decision by the Bucharest Court of Appeal. The suspect was detained on Tuesday by Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) and was subsequently brought before the court, which approved prosecutors’ request for pre-trial detention. According to DIICOT, the investigation found that between February and July 2026, the suspect allegedly gathered military-related information in preparation for diversion and sabotage operations. He reportedly identified and monitored military objectives and collected information on Romanian and allied armed forces. The suspect also allegedly took and transmitted photographs showing military equipment and the movement of personnel and combat equipment at several Romanian and multinational military bases located in Cluj, Constanta, Calarasi and Ilfov counties, as well as in Bucharest. DIICOT said the activities, by their nature, posed a threat to Romania’s national security. Investigation uncovered alleged links to Russian-directed networks The Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said the alleged sabotage operation was prevented through cooperation between Romanian intelligence and law-enforcement institutions, including DIICOT, the Interior Ministry’s Directorate for Combating Organised Crime and the Defence Ministry’s General Directorate for Defence Intelligence. SRI also said that foreign partner intelligence services were involved in the effort. According to the intelligence service, the Russian citizen had been under SRI surveillance since February 2026 as part of a wider investigation into alleged attempts to carry out diversion operations on Romanian territory. The investigation reportedly included the documentation of communications centres and military bases belonging to Romania and NATO allies, as well as headquarters of institutions belonging to the country’s national defence, public order and national security system. SRI said the case revealed an operational pattern similar to that allegedly used by Russian-linked sabotage networks in other European countries. The intelligence service also referred to previous cases uncovered in Romania in 2024 and 2025. Ukrainian aircraft allegedly among targets According to SRI, the suspect allegedly received instructions from an intermediary to produce photo and video material documenting strategic military objectives. The intelligence service said the targets included Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft while they were present on Romanian territory. SRI further claimed that the investigation showed that Russia continues to recruit individuals considered to be in vulnerable circumstances to carry out such activities. The case comes amid heightened concerns across Europe over alleged Russian-linked sabotage, espionage and other forms of hybrid activity targeting critical infrastructure and military-related facilities. Romanian authorities have stepped up cooperation between intelligence, law-enforcement and defence institutions in response to such threats, particularly in the context of Russia’s war against Ukraine and Romania’s role as a NATO member and a key logistical hub on the alliance’s eastern flank. The Russian citizen will remain in pre-trial detention for 30 days under Tuesday’s court decision. The allegations remain subject to judicial proceedings, and the suspect is presumed innocent until a final court ruling. DIICOT Statement Representatives of the Directorate for the Investigation of Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) said: On September 8, 2026, prosecutors with the Directorate for the Investigation of Organised Crime and Terrorism – Central Structure ordered the detention of a 40-year-old defendant, a Russian citizen, who is being investigated for the offence of attempted acts of diversion . The evidence gathered in the case indicates that, between February and July 2026, in preparation for carrying out hybrid acts of diversion/sabotage, under the direct coordination of an individual with whom he maintained contact through encrypted online messaging services, the defendant identified, monitored and collected military-related information. He also took and transmitted photographs concerning Romanian/allied armed forces equipment and the movement of personnel and military equipment at several Romanian and multinational military facilities (bases) located in Cluj, Constanta, Calarasi and Ilfov counties, as well as in the municipality of Bucharest. By their nature, these activities endangered national security. The Bucharest Court of Appeal is to be notified with a request for the defendant to be placed under pre-trial arrest for a period of 30 days. The judicial activities were carried out together with judicial police officers from DIICOT – Central Structure, the Directorate for Combating Organised Crime and its subordinate units. The operation benefited from intelligence support provided by the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) and assistance from the specialised structure within the General Directorate for Defence Intelligence (DGIA). We emphasise that throughout the entire criminal proceedings, the persons under investigation are entitled to all procedural rights and guarantees provided for by the Code of Criminal Procedure, as well as to the presumption of innocence. https://www.dw.com/en/india-urges-russia.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OFwI Attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crews Image: UGC/AFP Advertisement India has urged both Russia and Ukraine to ensure safe passage for commercial shipping through the Black Sea , as attacks on merchant vessels put Indian seafarers at risk and threaten to disrupt vital food and energy supplies. New Delhi says discussions with both sides are under way. "The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways must be restored at the earliest," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said last week. India accounts for more than 12% of the global seafaring workforce, with 311,936 maritime professionals, according to a 2026 industry report. And attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crews. The Turkish-owned MV Royad Mammadov, a cargo ship carrying grain from Ukraine, caught fire and sank following an attack on Monday , killing two crew members. The three Indian nationals aboard the vessel survived, but sustained injuries and were taken to Romania to receive medical treatment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for launching the strike. The Defense Ministry in Moscow separately said it had struck two Ukrainian cargo vessels in the Black Sea but did not specifically identify the ships. The Liberian-flagged oil tanker Aframax Rio was also recently attacked by unmanned vessels off Russia's Black Sea coast near Sochi, according to Russian authorities. The vessel was carrying 23 Indians, but all of them were rescued. How India has become Russia's trade lifeline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Can diplomacy deliver safety? Anil Wadhwa, a former Indian diplomat, said India's proposal to halt attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea covered energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain and energy exports, and an end to strikes on merchant vessels. "Securing an ironclad guarantee depends entirely on a broader cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in the maritime theater," Wadhwa told DW. India's close relations with Russia and expanding engagement with Ukraine give New Delhi access to both sides, but do not guarantee either will honor a shipping arrangement. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has described India's proposal for a possible ceasefire with Russia as the "broadest" of the four offers Kyiv has received. Russia has not publicly endorsed a binding safe-passage deal proposed by India, despite welcoming New Delhi's peace efforts. Rajan Kumar of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University said India could use its diplomatic leverage with Moscow to help bring the two sides towards an agreement. "India could play a constructive role in facilitating dialogue between Russia and Ukraine, particularly on the issue of ensuring the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea," Kumar told DW. How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Working with other powers to reach a deal He argued that India should also work with other influential countries from the Global South, particularly China, Brazil and South Africa. "A coordinated approach with these countries could enhance their collective diplomatic leverage and strengthen their capacity to persuade both parties to adopt mutually acceptable arrangements for maritime security," said Kumar. India's initiative comes as US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend , although its scope and implementation mechanism remain unclear. Harsh Pant, vice president of the New Delhi-based think tank Observer Research Foundation, said Trump's intervention could help India's efforts but might produce a narrower agreement that fails to address New Delhi's wider concerns. "The energy ceasefire could be an initial confidence-building measure, whereas a Black Sea shipping arrangement requires additional commitments on attacks against merchant vessels, ports, maritime routes and the security of commercial traffic," Pant told DW. "India need not compete with Washington for the public credit of mediation. It could instead press for the inclusion of broader maritime provisions in any US agreement,” he added. Will India face a higher import bill? Wadhwa said the proposed energy truce could also benefit Indian seafarers if it secured safe passage for energy cargoes. "Although Ukraine alleges that the Russians have already breached this so-called truce, there will be pressure on both sides to allow energy cargoes safe passage. India is bound to gain as far as its crews are concerned in such a scenario," he said. The disruption to Black Sea shipping also has other implications for India such as delays in shipments of key commodities and higher transport costs. "A prolonged Black Sea disruption would elevate India's import bill mainly via higher freight on Russian crude and constrained soft oil supplies, with the strongest near-term transmission to domestic edible oil prices and food inflation," said Lekha Chakraborty, professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/23/flas.text: Torrential rain has triggered flash flooding across southeast Queensland, Australia, breaking multiple October rainfall records, stranding drivers, forcing school closures and prompting hundreds of emergency calls over two days.The deluge began on Thursday with a water treatment plant near Moreton Bay, north of Brisbane, recording more than 250 millimetres of rain in 24 hours.Some locations received nearly 180 millimetres in just three hours. Beerburrum recorded its wettest October day on record, while Toowoomba experienced its heaviest October rainfall in 29 years.Flooded roads damaged infrastructure, disrupted electricity supplies and forced 14 schools to close.Authorities urged residents in parts of Caboolture and Burpengary to prepare to evacuate as a fresh wave of rain struck southeast Queensland on Friday, compounding the damage.Reporter jumps into floodwater to rescue trapped driverOne of the most dramatic moments of the crisis unfolded in Morayfield on Thursday, when Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reporter Will Murray and a bystander jumped into floodwaters to rescue a driver trapped in a rapidly sinking car.Murray told the ABC that the vehicle began to float and sink within seconds of driving into the flooded road, leaving no time to wait for emergency services.“My colleague and I sort of started to watch him sink further into the water and thought, ‘well, we don’t have time to wait,’” Murray said.“So I threw off my shoes, gave my glasses to my colleague and jumped in and started swimming. And thankfully somebody nearby jumped in with me to give me a hand.”The pair initially tried to break the car’s rear windscreen but were forced to move to the side of the vehicle. What Murray saw through the back window made the urgency clear.“Couldn’t get that door open. Got up onto the ute tray, looked through the back window and you could see that the water was up sort of shoulder level, sort of towards chin level, just terrifying and angling down,” he said.They eventually managed to open a door and pull the driver to safety. No injuries were reported.Authorities had already issued flood warnings across the area.At least eight weather stations recorded more than 300 millimetres of rainfall between Wednesday and Friday morning, more than three times the volume originally forecast by the Bureau of Meteorology.Wet conditions are expected to persist into the weekend, with forecasters warning of another peak on Monday and a cold front potentially shifting the weather pattern later in the week.Parts of New South Wales are now also in the path of the storm system.

https://www.dw.com/en/egypt-orders-closu.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Oktu Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was briefly detained after an Egyptian court ordered the closure of her news outlet [FILE: December 28, 2020] Image: Khaled Desouki/AFP Advertisement An Egyptian court on Tuesday ordered the closure of independent news website Mada Masr after convicting its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah , of operating without a license. Attalah, one of Egypt 's most prominent journalists, was detained for several hours following the verdict before being released after paying a fine. The court imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,400; €48,112), the maximum penalty for the offense. It also ordered the website to shut down and its equipment to be confiscated. Mada Masr, founded in 2013, is one of Egypt's few remaining independent news outlets. It is known for investigating corruption, human rights violations and the military's powerful role in the country. What happened during Lina Attalah's trial? Attalah's lawyers said the court rejected their requests to review the case file and submit additional evidence during Tuesday's hearing in Cairo. According to Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the hearing, the judge then appointed a new lawyer to represent Attalah despite objections from her eight-person defense team. "In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer, who had not uttered a single word, and entered them into the official record," Bahgat told news agency AFP. The judge announced the verdict amid protests from the defense before security officers detained Attalah. She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari confirmed. The outlet plans to appeal the closure order. During her release procedures, Attalah also learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in a separate case in 2024 to one year in prison and a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds. That conviction concerned charges of spreading false news and operating an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged the ruling, with a new hearing scheduled for November 11. Why has Egypt targeted Mada Masr? Mada Masr has faced years of legal battles with Egyptian authorities, who have blocked access to its website inside the country since 2017. The outlet says it first applied for a license in 2018 but received no response. It only learned that its application had been rejected when prosecutors raised the issue during another case in 2022. Mada Masr challenged that decision and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023. Six cases have been brought against the outlet and its journalists over the past six years, but Tuesday's trial was the first of its kind. Egyptian authorities maintain that the country respects freedom of expression but insist that media organizations must comply with the law, protect national security and counter misinformation. How have press freedom groups reacted? The ruling drew widespread international condemnation. A coalition of 119 rights organizations and media outlets, including Amnesty International , Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), described the prosecution as an "unprecedented attack on press freedom." "Today's decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country," Amnesty International said. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called the ruling "outrageous" and "shameful." "If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe," said CPJ regional director Sara Qudah. US Senator Chris Van Hollen also criticized the prosecution, describing the charges as baseless and saying that "journalism is not a crime." What is the state of press freedom in Egypt? The case comes amid a broader crackdown on independent journalism. Six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash were arrested in September and subsequently charged with terrorism-related offenses. Authorities accuse them of links to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and spreading false information to undermine confidence in state institutions and encourage protests. The journalists have reported being tortured following their arrests, according to EIPR. Egypt's Interior Ministry has denied the allegations. On Tuesday, prosecutors extended their pretrial detention by another 15 days. Rights groups warn that such detention can continue for months or even years. According to EIPR, Egypt currently holds 26 journalists in connection with their work. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters View image in fullscreen The bill is being championed by Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party and is strongly backed by its far-right coalition partner, the League. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters Italy ‘Like priests who don’t believe in God’: Italy’s anti-vax medics eye return to frontline duty Progress of bill to reinstate struck-off doctors hinged on support from far right figure Roberto Vannacci, whose rise is shaping politics before 2027 elections Angela Giuffrida in Rome Thu 12 Nov 2026 05.20 EST Last modified on Thu 12 Nov 2026 06.01 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A ntonio Cremasco contracted Covid at a dinner party on 6 March 2020. Four days later, as Italy became the first European country to go into nationwide lockdown, he was fighting for his life. “I spent 20 days in intensive care, followed by another 20 days in a hospital ward,” said Cremasco, from Bassano del Grappa in the northern Italian Veneto region. After leaving hospital, he needed oxygen therapy for another six months. Cremasco’s ordeal was such that when Covid vaccines became available in Italy in early 2021, he had no qualms about being vaccinated, and he believes the decision saved his life once again. “All those who had been in intensive care with me died,” he said. “Without the vaccine, if I had caught Covid again, I had a high risk of dying too.” View image in fullscreen Doctors treating Covid patients in an intensive care unit at a Rome hospital in March 2020. Photograph: Antonio Masiello/Getty Images But Cremasco, who is now 76 and recently received his annual Covid and winter flu jab, has struggled to convince his vaccine-sceptic son, a father of two, of the drugs’ safety. He said he and his wife were wary of having their potentially unvaccinated grandchildren in their home whenever the children were ill, fearing for their own health. “They always seem to be sick,” Cremasco said. His family rift mirrors a wider divide over vaccination in Italy, which has been brought back to the political spotlight by a controversial bill approved in October in the lower house of parliament. The measure allows healthcare workers who were struck off their professional registers during the pandemic for serious violations connected to their anti-vaccination beliefs – for example, promoting treatments that lacked a scientific basis – to apply to be reinstated. The bill is being championed by the prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party and is strongly backed by its far-right coalition partner, the League. But with allies in Forza Italia split, its approval in the lower house hinged on support from National Future (FN), a rival far-right force led by the former army general Roberto Vannacci, whose emergence is shaping the political landscape before general elections next year. Vannacci has voiced opposition to vaccine mandates, and his rhetoric frequently targets the vaccine-sceptic audience. View image in fullscreen Roberto Vannacci, president of Futuro Nazionale, attends a rally in Milan on 2 November. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Getty Images The measure still needs to clear the senate, with a vote scheduled in January. But its progress has alarmed medical experts, less because of the number of healthcare workers involved – it is believed to be very small – and more because of the risk of further eroding trust in vaccines. Nearly one in two Italian adults are hesitant about vaccination, according to a report by the department of public health and paediatric sciences at the University of Turin published in the Lancet Regional Health Europe in February. The report, which sampled 50,000 adults across Italy, found the ambivalence was driven more by misinformation and lack of institutional trust than by fears over vaccine safety. “Political communication and the lack of trust among Italians in institutions carry a significant weight,” said Roberta Siliquini, the head of the school of hygiene and preventive medicine at the University of Turin and the report’s chief researcher. “There really is a disinformation campaign in this sense – and those who want to disinform are very good at communicating.” The implications are being profoundly felt: this year there has been a resurgence in measles, with 472 infections reported during the first five months, compared with 322 in the same period last year, according to health ministry figures. More than half of the cases were reported in young adults. Take-up of the flu vaccine among people aged 65 and over so far this season has dipped to 49.81% , the first time it has fallen below 50% since the winter of 2014-15. In August, a four-year-old child in Palermo, Sicily, died of diphtheria. Her parents reportedly told doctors they had not vaccinated her because her cousin was autistic and they were convinced vaccines were the reason. There is no evidence of any link between autism and vaccines. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators clash with police officers during a protest against the government’s introduction of the Covid ‘green pass’ in Rome on 9 October 2021. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters Siquilini said the tragic case was a reminder of the responsibility that everyone, “but especially politicians”, had to deliver the correct message on vaccines. She warned that the rehabilitation of those who rejected scientific evidence could have a “devastating” impact on how people perceived vaccines. The message has been repeatedly undermined. On 28 October, a day after the lower house vote, Claudio Borghi, a League politician, came under fire for hosting an anti-vaccine seminar in the senate. Later in the day, in what was believed to have been an indirect rebuke, the Italian president, Sergio Mattarella used a speech during a high-profile cancer research gathering to condemn the spread of anti-vax messages while warning against “irrational beliefs” and “destructive fake news”. Borghi has proposed revising a law introduced in 2017 by the then leftwing government that extended the number of obligatory childhood vaccinations from four to 10, adding, for example, one against pertussis, or whooping cough. He has defended his position, arguing he is not anti-vaccine but that mandatory vaccines “lead to resistance”. View image in fullscreen A group protesting against the use of the green pass and the restrictions that were to come into effect for unvaccinated people in July 2021. Photograph: Lorenzo Palizzolo/Getty Images As for the reinstatement of the medics struck off during the pandemic, he told the Guardian that the proposal’s aim was “to foster reconciliation after all these years”. He said: “In our view, nobody should lose their job because of a personal belief.” Scepticism over vaccinations took root in Italy in the late 1990s, as in many other countries, mainly driven by now debunked claims of a connection between the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination and autism. The arrival of social media accelerated the spread of vaccine misinformation, contributing to a drop in immunisation rates against preventable diseases. The 2017 move to make childhood vaccinations obligatory further emboldened anti-vaccine groups while creating fertile ground for rightwing populist parties, including the Five Star Movement (M5S), which continued to spread misinformation about vaccines after coming to power in 2018, and before the realities of the pandemic forced a shift in tone. Now in opposition, M5S is highly critical of the move to re-embrace anti-vax healthcare workers. Lorenzo Mattia Signori, a nurse in Veneto, said politicians were “opportunists” and Meloni’s coalition was simply trying to draw votes from anti-vax voters as it eyed a second mandate. Signori, who is also a regional secretary for Cittadinanzattiva, an association focused on patient advocacy, including pushing for campaigns to inform citizens about vaccine benefits, said: “Ensuring that people get vaccinated is the largest prevention system we have. If everyone gets sick instead, the Italian healthcare system would not hold.” He hopes that Mattarella will use his power as president to stop the anti-vaccine medics measure from being signed into law. “We cannot have them in hospitals,” he said. “It would be like going to church and hearing a priest who says he doesn’t believe in God.” Explore more on these topics Italy Europe Vaccines and immunisation news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
